awd_titl_txt: CAS: Promoting Selective CO2 Electroreduction by Active Site Engineering
awd_abstract_narration:
With the support of the Chemical Catalysis program in the Division of Chemistry, Dr. Anthony Shoji Hall at Johns Hopkins University is studying methods to improve the performance of catalysts to enable storing renewable energy in the form of chemical bonds. Energy storage devices are important for curbing catastrophic climate change. However, renewable electricity from wind and solar is intermittent, which means that this energy must be stored for use at night or when the wind is not blowing. The electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to chemical fuels is a potential strategy for storing renewable electricity. Catalysts usually exhibit variations in performance when the structure of the material is changed. The proposed study will use experimental methods to understand how the structure of the material influences its performance as a catalyst. Dr. Hall's laboratory also actively engages in outreach at inner city Baltimore high schools. This activity will allow a female minority high school student to study in his laboratory to learn about renewable energy science.

With the support of the Chemical Catalysis program in the Division of Chemistry, Dr. Anthony Shoji Hall at Johns Hopkins University is studying the structure-property relationships of nano-structured materials for electrochemical CO2 reduction. Nanomaterials exhibit a broad distribution of sites – such as edges, corners, and terraces – which can exhibit different reactivity. This proposal focuses on preparing catalysts with well-defined populations of active sites by coating defect sites or terrace sites with inert metal oxides; potentially allowing the experimentalist to unambiguously connect catalyst structure to property. Electrochemical kinetic measurements and surface enhanced in-situ infrared absorption spectroscopy (SEIRAS) will be used to interrogate the reaction mechanism of catalysts with well-defined active site structures. Knowledge obtained from these studies will be used to develop materials that promote more efficient catalytic pathways.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project investigated how the atomic structure and reaction environment of catalysts control their ability to convert carbon dioxide into useful fuels and chemicals. The work is motivated by the need to develop efficient, stable, and selective processes that can recycle carbon and store renewable electricity in chemical form.

Scientific Outcomes (Intellectual Merit):

We also studied palladium-bismuth (Pd₃Bi) alloys in several different atomic arrangements. Although the composition was identical, only the disordered alloy was highly active, while the ordered structure was inactive. This demonstrated clearly that the arrangement of atoms, not just the elements present, determines catalytic behavior.

We showed that controlling how much water is available in the reaction environment can steer the reaction toward making more complex multicarbon products such as ethylene, ethanol, and propanol. By lowering the effective water activity in the electrolyte, we achieved about 73 percent efficiency for multicarbon products on unmodified copper catalysts. This introduced water management as a new tool for directing reaction outcomes.

Finally, we developed a copper-zinc intermetallic catalyst, ε-CuZn₄, that achieved more than 80 percent efficiency for converting CO₂ into carbon monoxide at relatively low energy input. This material outperformed pure zinc, which is less stable under operating conditions. Spectroscopic measurements  showed that copper helps stabilize zinc against oxidation and modifies its electronic structure in a way that promotes carbon monoxide production.

Broader Impacts:
The project contributed to long-term societal goals by advancing methods to recycle carbon dioxide into useful products. These findings may support future technologies for clean energy storage and sustainable chemical manufacturing.

The award also created training opportunities for graduate students and undergraduates, who gained experience in catalyst synthesis, spectroscopy, and electrochemical testing. Two high school students from Baltimore participated in a structured summer research program in the laboratory. They worked closely with graduate students on electrodeposition experiments and presented their results at the end of the program. One of these students later received national recognition in the Samsung Solve for Tomorrow competition.
